# He Sang Both Parts

In 1986, ornithologists hiked into the Alakaʻi Wilderness Preserve — a rain-soaked plateau more than three thousand feet above Kauaʻi's beaches, where the trees drip constantly and the mud swallows boots whole — carrying microphones toward the last Kauaʻi ʻōʻō on Earth.

The ʻōʻō was a small, sooty bird, fist-sized, with a slender curved bill and tufts of golden feathers at its thighs, a nectar feeder that moved through the flowers of the native forest the way its honeyeater cousins move through gardens on the other side of the Pacific. For most of a century, science had filed its family, the mohoids, among the waxwings and orioles of the mainland. DNA eventually corrected the record in the most astonishing way possible: their true relatives are the honeyeaters of Australia and the islands, birds whose ancestors made some improbable voyage across thousands of miles of open ocean to found a dynasty in Hawaii. The ʻōʻōs were that dynasty's great triumph, and by 1986 it was nearly finished. The Oʻahu ʻōʻō vanished in the 1830s. The Hawaiʻi ʻōʻō in 1934. The Kauaʻi ʻōʻō was the family's last representative anywhere on the planet.

By then he was a male, and by then he was alone. His mate, by most accounts, was lost in Hurricane ʻIwa in 1982, which scoured the plateau and shredded the forest understory; the pigs and rats and mosquito-borne malaria did the rest, unraveling a place that had held together for millions of years. But ʻōʻō pairs sang duets — intricate, coordinated songs in which the male's phrases and the female's phrases interleaved like hands folding together. And this male sang both parts. He sang the duet alone, the way a person might waltz alone in an empty ballroom, faithfully performing both steps of a dance no one would ever join.

The recording captures it: a voice, clear and unhurried, calling phrase after phrase into a forest that could not answer. The tape lives in a sound archive at Cornell now. You can find it in ten seconds and listen to a bird that has been gone since 1987. It is, as far as anyone knows, the only animal in history to have its duet preserved in the act of singing both halves — a courtship and an elegy in the same breath, performed for a microphone by a bird who did not know the difference.

A sound that outlived its own world.

⁂

Sound is the most perishable thing there is. Consider Krakatoa. In August 1883 the volcano detonated itself out of existence, and the blast was the loudest sound in recorded history — sailors forty miles away had their eardrums ruptured; the report was clearly heard nearly three thousand miles distant on the island of Rodrigues; the barometric pressure wave lapped around the entire planet several times. It may be the closest anything has come to a universal sound, audible across an impossible fraction of the Earth. And by evening it was gone. Not faint — gone. The loudest noise ever made left not one atom of itself behind. There is no such thing as residual sound. A sound exists only in the act of its making; to sound and to perish are, for sound, the same event.

Almost everything else survives death. A museum drawer can hold a bird's bones, its skin, its eggs, even its DNA, arranged in ghostly order of decreasing form. You can stuff a skin. You can sequence a genome. You cannot stuff a song. Which is what makes recordings so strange — a rip in the rules, a voice without a body, presence detached from the present moment. An archive of extinct sounds is the only place in the natural world where the dead can be caught mid-breath.

⁂

The vast majority of extinction happened before microphones, which means the majority of the dead are silent in a way we rarely pause to notice.

The great auk — flightless, penguin-like, absurdly trusting — was finally finished off in June 1844, when the last breeding pair was killed on a skerry off Iceland. Contemporary accounts describe its voice as a low croaking, a weird gargle. That is all we have: three words of description. Nobody alive has heard it; nobody ever will. The moa of New Zealand, nine species of them, some towering twice the height of a person, are entirely beyond recovery as sound. So are the elephant birds of Madagascar, eggs the size of basketballs, voices beyond even conjecture.

And then the passenger pigeon, which may be the most staggering acoustic loss of all. It was likely the most abundant bird that ever lived, numbering in the billions. In 1813 Audubon watched a single passing column for days and gave up on counting; the flocks were said to darken the sky at noon and to take hours to pass over a fixed point. Witnesses described the sound of those multitudes not really as birdsong but as weather — a rushing, thunderous roar of wings, a living storm front. Martha, the last of them, died at the Cincinnati Zoo on September 1, 1914. Not one second of tape exists. The sound of billions of wings — a weather system that will never again exist over the Ohio Valley — simply evaporated from the Earth, and the absence doesn't even have a place in our imagination, because no one who heard it left more than adjectives.

The technology arrived just in time for almost no one. In 1889, an eight-year-old German boy named Ludwig Koch recorded a shama thrush singing on an Edison phonograph — the first known recording of any wild animal's voice, as far as anyone can tell. Koch grew up to become one of the great natural-history sound recordists of the century at the BBC. In 1935, two Cornell ornithologists hauled recording gear into the Singer Tract of Louisiana and captured ivory-billed woodpeckers — the flat, nasal, trumpet-like *kent* calls, plus the double knocks on dead trees. That bird is now probably gone; its voice is not. There is something almost unbearable about this particular arrangement: the bird's body failed, but its voice sits on a shelf, patient, ready.

Other cases are stranger. New Zealand's huia, that astonishing bird with two differently shaped bills in one species, was effectively extinct by the first years of the twentieth century. The only recording that survives is not the huia at all — it is a man, in 1909, whistling an imitation of the bird's call. An echo of a second order. Our entire acoustic memory of the huia is a human throat standing in for a vanished one. The thylacine, the Tasmanian tiger, left us grainy film of the last known individual pacing its concrete cage in 1933 — but not, as far as anyone knows, a single second of its voice. We can watch it breathe. We cannot hear it.

And the soundless dead outnumber even these many, many times over, because until roughly 1860, no human voice was ever captured by anything. Every person who ever lived before the machine — Socrates, Shakespeare, Joan of Arc, your great-great-grandmother singing over a cradle — contributed exactly zero seconds to the record. We have their handwriting, their portraits, their words on paper. Nothing they said aloud, ever, to anyone.

We have learned to approximate. Scholars read Hittite, the oldest attested Indo-European language, aloud in reconstructed pronunciation — plausible, but a best guess assembled from spelling habits, comparative evidence, and meter. Linguists speak reconstructed Proto-Indo-European in seminar rooms, performing a language no one ever spoke, an average of ghosts. The Hurrian hymn to Nikkal, around 3,400 years old, is the oldest substantially notated music we have; recordings of it exist, and no two versions agree, because the tablet preserves the skeleton of the melody and the flesh is lost forever. There are Sumerian lullabies we can sound out syllable by syllable, four thousand years old, mothers' words for tired children — with the tunes unknowable. Reconstruction is a kind of informed séance: real voices, dimly, through the veil of arithmetic and spelling.

⁂

Here is the uncomfortable part: the losses are not all in the past, and they are not only about species. Quiet itself is becoming an extinct sound.

The acoustic ecologist Gordon Hempton has spent decades hunting for genuine quiet, and by his count only a handful of places remain in the continental United States where you can sit for a quarter of an hour without a single human-made sound intruding. His listening post of choice is in the Hoh Rain Forest of Olympic National Park, on the far, wet edge of Washington State, where he established a spot called One Square Inch of Silence. The geometry is the problem: a jet at cruising altitude is audible for miles in every direction, which means that protecting a square inch of quiet requires, in effect, negotiating with the entire sky. Silence, it turns out, is not the absence of sound but an ecosystem operating at full volume — every layer of it, insect to owl to wind — and it has a habitat, and the habitat is shrinking.

The ocean is louder, too. Commercial shipping has filled the low frequencies with propeller noise; by some estimates, ambient background in those bands has crept upward relentlessly since the mid-twentieth century. Blue whale calls have drifted downward in frequency over decades — researchers still argue about why — and whatever the cause, the distances those songs evolved to cross are being filled in with engine hum. A whale singing across an ocean basin is shouting into a room that people keep turning up.

The sound recordist Bernie Krause proposed what he called the niche hypothesis: in a healthy habitat, species divide the acoustic spectrum the way lanes divide a highway, each voice occupying its own band so that everyone can be heard. The dawn chorus is not a mob scene; it is a meticulously partitioned bandwidth, evolved over millennia. Krause recorded a Sierra Nevada meadow before and after what loggers called selective cutting. To a visitor's ear, the after sounded much the same — birds, wind, a stream. On the spectrogram, the plot of sound over time, the world had visibly emptied. The meadow sounded fine and was not fine. Biodiversity loss has an acoustics, and you have to know how to hear it. The writer Robert Pyle called the broader phenomenon the extinction of experience: what goes extinct first is not the species but the encounter, and what we never meet, we never mourn.

⁂

So why do people keep climbing into swamps with microphones? Not, mostly, for science alone. Recording is attention made portable. An archive of sound is a wager that listening matters — that someone, someday, will want to hear what a frog chorus sounded like in a wetland that is now a parking structure, or a dawn chorus from a forest that has since thinned. Cornell's Macaulay Library holds hundreds of thousands of such recordings, many gathered for birds now gone or going, tape spun in something between curiosity and pre-grief.

Look at the comments under the Kauaʻi ʻōʻō recording sometime. Strangers keep arriving there, decades after the bird died, and leaving short messages of sorrow, as if at a headstone. Extinction usually reaches us as an inventory — numbers, dates, Latin names, causes. A recording makes it an absence with a shape: something you can put on, take off, and put on again, an elegy you can hold in your hand.

It's worth being honest about the archive, too. It skews toward the loud and the lovely — hours of nightingale, minutes of frog; the plain brown birds and the silent-seeming insects get less tape. We are still losing soundscapes faster than we capture them. Every sound archive, like every museum, is a mirror of what we managed to love in time.

⁂

The Kauaʻi ʻōʻō's inheritance is a strange one: a courtship song with no court, preserved at the exact moment it became an elegy, resurrected a little each time a stranger presses play. The bird meant it as an invitation. We receive it as a memorial. But those aren't as different as they seem, because a duet is a sound built for two, and the tape only ever held one of them. The other half has always been waiting somewhere else — in a listener.

He sang both parts because he had no choice. We do have one: to pay attention while attention can still matter, and to grieve out loud when it doesn't. Out there somewhere, a bird is singing a duet into the dark, hoping for a second voice. Press play. For two minutes, the forest has an audience again.

And for once, someone is listening.
